newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr rediscovers caution after wild rally.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr rediscovers caution after wild rally.

text.p: The Australian dollar held firm at the midsession although the local market was noticeably reluctant to extend its 1-1/3 cent offshore rally in the face of fresh offers above US$0.7540.

Dealers said investors were also understandably cautious in case today's Reserve Bank board meeting resulted in a rate cut this week. There has been a growing feeling the bank would hold off until late this month or August but, given it had surprised with three of its four cuts, the market was taking no chances. Austrlaia's balance of goods and services was a higher than forecast A$873 million surplus, aiding sentiment at the margin.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the currency had found a niche at US$0.7527/32 having topped out at US$0.7570 overnight after a blistering short covering rally from US$0.7453/58.
The initial spark reportedly came from a A$300 million buy order against the Canadian dollar from a U.S. IMM fund which triggered a mass of stops past US$0.7480 and US$0.7520.
Traders said it looked like the fund was taking profits on a short position established last week in the wake of a surprise rate hike by the Bank of Canada which saw AUD/CAD fall sharply.
They also suspected funds might be switching out of poorly performing C$ bonds into A$ debt where prospects were brighter.

Bonds here were buoyed by a very favourable inflation outlook -- underlying inflation is set to fall under the RBA's 2-3 percent target band in Q2 -- which in turn offered the chance of yet another cut in official interest rates.
The prospect was not so welcome to the A$ where short term interest differentials tended to dominate and domestic money rates had already moved below those on offer in the U.S.

The 90-day bank bill future for September stands at 94.86 implying a rate of 5.14 percent compared to the present 5.50 percent cash rate, while three month Eurodollar futures are at 94.12 reflecting market expectations U.S. rates will be raised.

Virtually no one in the market expects the Federal Reserve to move at its policy meeting this week, which runs today and Wednesday, but reckon the sheer strength of the economy will force a tightening in August or September.
This contrasted with the Australian experience where the economy had proved to be a lot softer than expected in recent months and where there were no capacity constraints on the horizon.
In this atmosphere there were few who would quibble were the RBA to ease tomorrow, which in turn made it hard for dealers to see the dollar sustaining a rally above US$0.7575 resistance.
Today's trade data added little to the policy outlook although it could be argued the persistent weakness of imports shown therein reflected the poor state of domestic demand.

Imports of goods fell 1.0 percent with by far the largest drop in the capital goods sector which slid 13 percent. That was a worrying sign for business investment, said analysts, and added to the case for another easing.

The overall surplus of A$873 million was way above forecasts of A$163 million, but boosted by the export of a A$500 million frigate. Even without the latter, the performance was good and net exports should make a big contribution to Q2 GDP growth.

More important from a policy point of view will be retail trade data for May on Tuesday. It was a shock 1.7 percent fall in sales for April which first started the market thinking about a fifth cut in RBA rates, so a bounce is needed this time to stop it looking for an immediate easing.
Median forecasts are for a rise of around 2.0 percent in May and anything less than a 1.0 percent gain would be considered soft.
Elsewhere, the dollar was up at 86.55/65 yen from 85.10/20 late Monday and at 57.3 in trade weighted terms from 56.7.
